abstract: Regeneration restores tissues lost to injury, but its consequences may extend beyond local repair. Whether regeneration produces lasting systemic effects on developmental timing and lifespan remains poorly understood. Here we investigated the long-term consequences of repeated regeneration in the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii. To determine these consequences, we repeatedly amputated juveniles at monthly intervals, removing approximately half of the body after each regenerative cycle, and compared them with control unamputated siblings. Repeatedly regenerating worms lived approximately 1.5-fold longer than controls and showed delayed sexual maturation, including delayed gametogenic progression at the morphological and transcriptional levels. Somatic progression was also delayed, as indicated by slower accumulation of pigmentation associated with developmental progression, while regenerative competence was maintained across amputations. To investigate whether regeneration engages distant tissues, we compared head transcriptomes from amputated and unamputated worms. Posterior amputation altered head gene expression within 2 hours, including increased expression of genes associated with younger head profiles, such as igf-like and alpha-tubulin. Together, our results show that repeated regeneration not only restores lost tissues but prolongs the juvenile state, delays reproductive and somatic maturation, and extends lifespan, a phenomenon we term the Highlander effect. These findings suggest that regeneration may influence organismal life history beyond tissue replacement, with neurohormonal signaling as a potential mediator.
